title: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Pre-natal and post-natal growth”. Scope: human foetus

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Gestational age and fetal linear dimensions are available in modern longitudinal growth resources. Standard smooth growth models can estimate the timing of peak velocity, though harmonizing length measures introduces some uncertainty.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit fetal length against gestational age with a smooth curve and locate the maximum first derivative or zero second derivative. A velocity peak near gestational month five supports the claim; a well-estimated peak at a materially different time or monotonic velocity refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Gestational dating and choice of length proxy affect inflection estimates.

Ultrasound commonly measures crown-rump length only early and long-bone dimensions later.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.95
data existence: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fetal size by week of gestation is tabulated in a large public standard, and locating a velocity maximum is a direct calculation. The fifth-month inflection is specific enough to fail if the peak lies elsewhere. The remaining weakness is that the measured length is often a skeletal segment rather than whole-body length, so the test is exact only if that proxy tracks the length Thompson plotted. That is a limited measurement issue, not a missing dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate human fetal length velocity by gestational age. A maximum near the fifth month, with velocity rising before it and falling after, would support the claim. A maximum far from that month, or no inflection, would refute it. Femur length or crown-rump length may stand in for crown-heel length if the two are shown to share the same velocity peak.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern standards usually record femur length or crown-rump length rather than the crown-heel length of the older curves.

Dating error and cross-sectional sampling can shift the apparent month of the inflection.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the human curve of growth in body length has its point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life, then the velocity of body-length growth (d length / d gestational age) must still be increasing through the end of the first trimester and must already be decreasing through the third trimester, so that the velocity maximum lies between the end of the first trimester and the start of the third (about 14 to 24 completed weeks of gestation, i.e. months 4-6, centred on month 5).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Median CRL (daily rows, 9+0 to 14+0 weeks) was differentiated numerically (np.gradient) to give velocity in mm/week and averaged over weeks 9-10 and 13-14. Median birth length of girls and boys (daily rows, 24+0 to 42+6 weeks) was averaged across sexes, converted to mm, differentiated, averaged by completed week, and compared between weeks 24-28 and 36-40, with an OLS trend over weeks 24-40. The femur-length median equation was differentiated analytically over 14-40 weeks and the age of maximum velocity located. The pre-registered decision rules were then applied.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Using the 50th-centile curves of international (INTERGROWTH-21st) standards for fetal crown-rump length (9+0 to 14+0 weeks) and for newborn crown-heel length by gestational age at birth (24 to 42 weeks), compute growth velocity in mm/week by finite differences of the median curve. The claim is supported if (a) median CRL velocity averaged over weeks 13-14 exceeds that averaged over weeks 9-10 (length growth still accelerating at 14 weeks), and (b) median crown-heel-length velocity averaged over weeks 24-28 exceeds that averaged over weeks 36-40 and the 24-40 velocity series has a negative linear trend (growth already decelerating from 24 weeks). (a) and (b) together bracket the velocity maximum within 14-24 weeks, which contains 'about the fifth month'. As a secondary check, the gestational age of peak velocity of INTERGROWTH-21st fetal femur length (14-40 weeks) is reported; a femur peak within 14-24 weeks or at the 14-week boundary is consistent with the claim.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if median CRL velocity is already lower at weeks 13-14 than at weeks 9-10 (velocity maximum before month 4, i.e. before 14 weeks), or if median crown-heel-length velocity at weeks 36-40 is not lower than at weeks 24-28 (velocity maximum after month 6), or if neither measure shows a change of sign in acceleration anywhere in 9-42 weeks (no inflection). A femur-length velocity peak later than 24 weeks also counts against the claim. Any other combination is 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: lower bound (weeks of gestation) of the bracket containing the body-length velocity maximum; upper bound 24 weeks by criterion (b)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: bracket 14-24 weeks from the pre-registered tests; the newborn series actually shows a plateau of ~12.5-13.5 mm/week from 24 to 33 weeks before velocity falls, so the data alone only place the maximum somewhere in 14-33 weeks

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson plots 'length' of the human foetus (crown-heel body length from His and other nineteenth-century sources) against age in months and locates an inflection about month five. No modern public standard measures crown-heel length continuously across gestation: ultrasound gives crown-rump length to 14 weeks and skeletal lengths afterwards, and body length is measured directly only at birth. The test therefore brackets the velocity peak from two body-length measures of the same consortium's population: crown-rump length (first trimester) and crown-heel length of newborns by gestational age at birth (24-42 weeks). Gestational ages are menstrual weeks; Thompson's 'fifth month' is taken as roughly 17-22 menstrual weeks, so months 4-6 (14-24 weeks) is the window consistent with 'about the fifth month'. Velocities of the median curve are used because the published standards are smoothed centile tables, not individual-level data. The rOpenSci gigs package redistributes the INTERGROWTH-21st published tables and equations as machine-readable files; those files are used, with the primary publications cited. No data values were inspected before this pre-registration.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
INTERGROWTH-21st international standard for early fetal size: crown-rump length for gestational age, centile table (Papageorghiou et al. 2014, Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol 44:641-648), as redistributed in the rOpenSci gigs R package

INTERGROWTH-21st newborn size standards (Villar et al. 2014, Lancet 384:857-868) and very preterm size at birth references (Villar et al. 2016, Lancet Glob Health 4:e681-e691): birth length by gestational age, centile tables by sex, as redistributed in gigs

INTERGROWTH-21st fetal growth standards, femur-length median equation (Papageorghiou et al. 2014, Lancet 384:869-879), as coded in gigs R/ig_fet.R

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both pre-registered pass conditions hold, but condition (b) is met only because velocity drops after 33 weeks: median birth length grows at an almost constant 12.5-13.5 mm/week from 24 to 33 weeks. The data therefore locate the velocity maximum somewhere between 14 and about 33 weeks (months 4-8), not sharply at month 5; Thompson's 'velocity tends to fall away' after month five is at best a gentle plateau until month 8.

The two body-length measures differ (crown-rump length before 14 weeks; crown-heel length at birth after 24 weeks) and there is a 10-week gap with no direct body-length standard, so no single smooth curve could be fitted.

Birth length by gestational age for 24-32 weeks comes from preterm births (a reference, not a prescriptive standard); preterm neonates may be smaller than fetuses of the same age still in utero, which would flatten the apparent early-third-trimester velocity.

Femur length, the only skeletal length standard spanning 14-40 weeks, has monotonically decreasing velocity from 14 weeks (peak at or before 14 weeks), i.e. a skeletal-segment inflection earlier than month 5; only whole-body length is tested as Thompson stated it.

The INTERGROWTH-21st tables are smoothed population centiles, so no individual-level uncertainty could be attached to the velocity estimates.

Gestational age conventions differ: INTERGROWTH-21st uses menstrual age; Thompson's nineteenth-century sources were probably dated from conception, a ~2-week offset that does not change the bracket.
